summary: Describes an experiment in automated resource sharing between unlike systems. A user of the MUDDLE system at MIT-DMS could make use of the MACSYMA algebra system at MIT-Mathlab without knowing anything about the network or MACSYMA.

plainLanguage.summary: A program on one computer quietly asked another computer's math program for help, so the user never noticed a second machine was involved.

subtitle: Using MACSYMA algebra system from MUDDLE, transparent to the user.

tldr.problem: Powerful mathematical computation resources like MACSYMA existed on the ARPANET, but using them from another system required manual steps and understanding of both systems.
tldr.mechanism: MIT-DMS built software in MUDDLE that automatically connects to MACSYMA, translates between MUDDLE and MACSYMA notation, sends commands, interprets results, and presents them back to the MUDDLE user. A user can call an INTEGRATE function as if it were local, and the system handles all network communication transparently.
tldr.outcome: Users of MUDDLE could use powerful MACSYMA capabilities without knowing about the network, MACSYMA, or having to manually manage the remote connection. Parts of a single computation could be split between systems.

facts.label: Notation conversion
facts.value: MUDDLE prefix form <-> MACSYMA infix form

today: RFC 578 describes an experiment in automated resource sharing over the ARPANET. It demonstrates early concepts in transparent remote procedure calls and system integration across networks. It is not a standard or specification.

sections.title: Automated Resource Sharing
sections.content: The MUDDLE system at MIT-DMS is a general-purpose environment for automatic programming, graphics, and computation. MACSYMA at MIT-Mathlab is a specialized system for symbolic mathematics: integration, differentiation, equation solving, and complex transformations. Rather than requiring users to manually switch systems and copy data, MIT-DMS created an experiment in automated resource sharing. When a MUDDLE user calls a mathematical function that MUDDLE cannot compute, the system automatically reaches across the ARPANET to MACSYMA, gets the answer, converts the result back to MUDDLE form, and returns it to the user. The user never needs to know this happened.
sections.plainLanguage: A MUDDLE user can ask for a mathematical operation. The MUDDLE system secretly calls MACSYMA on another computer, gets the answer, and hands it back as if MUDDLE did the work.

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content: The resource-sharing system has several integrated parts: connecting to Mathlab and logging in, converting MUDDLE notation to MACSYMA notation (prefix form to infix form), sending commands to MACSYMA, interpreting the results, converting answers back to MUDDLE form, and handling disconnection. When a MUDDLE user types <INTEGRATE '<* .X 3>>$ (integrate 3 times X in MUDDLE notation), the system converts it to STRING (INTEGRATE (3*X,X)) for MACSYMA, sends it over TELNET, interprets MACSYMA's output, converts the answer back to MUDDLE prefix form, and returns </ <* 3 <^ .X 2>> 2> (3X squared divided by 2). The system supports INTEGRATE, SIMPLIFY, DIFF, EXPAND, and other mathematical functions, and can handle optional parameters like the variable to integrate with respect to.
sections.plainLanguage: MUDDLE translates math problems to MACSYMA's language, MACSYMA solves them, and MUDDLE translates the answer back and shows it to the user.

sections.title: User Experience
sections.content: In normal TERSE mode, the user sees only the result. In VERBOSE mode, the user can see the complete interaction between MUDDLE and MACSYMA for debugging. If the user wants direct control, they can type <TELCOM 1>$ to enter manual communication with MACSYMA. A user can also display graphs using MUDDLE's graphics capabilities with results from MACSYMA, for example drawing the derivative of X cubed across a range of values. If MACSYMA becomes confused, the user can type <DIS>$ to disconnect and start fresh.
sections.plainLanguage: Users see only the answers by default. If they want to watch the conversation between computers, they can. They can also take direct control or drop the connection if something goes wrong.

references.text: Parrish, S. and Pickens, J., "MIT-MATHLAB Meets UCSB-OLS", NWG/RFC 525, NIC 17161.
